assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, built on Katori's magic-wavelength proposal, trap many neutral atoms in a Lamb-Dicke regime and reach fractional uncertainties near 1e-18. This is the leading platform for the next definition of the second, for relativistic geodesy and for tests of fundamental constants. The idea is conceptually clean and the impact is large. In laser spectroscopy, controlling the light shift so the trapping field drops out is exactly the kind of idea that changes what can be measured.
assessment.attribution: Katori made the decisive proposal and first demonstrations of the magic-wavelength lattice clock. Ye's group brought it to record accuracy and stability and added many-body and cavity-stabilised-laser developments. A two-person prize is clean. Credit for the Sr clock also extends to others (e.g. Takamoto, Ido, Lemonde, Ludlow), which the supplied names do not cover.
assessment.maturity: Independent confirmation across several groups and species (Sr, Yb, Hg), with international comparisons and dedicated redefinition roadmaps. The comb and ion-trap clocks were recognised in 2005 and 2012, so the timing is natural. The field is mature but still advancing.
uncertainties: Whether the committee wants to credit Ye mainly for clocks or for the comb and clock-laser work.
Ido and Takamoto may be considered for the first lattice-clock demonstration; I cannot verify the priority details from the supplied text.
The second has not yet been redefined, so one could argue the final impact is still pending.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Cirac-Zoller proposal for ion-trap quantum gates, its realisation in trapped-ion processors and the quantum simulation concepts have shaped the whole quantum-information field. They were the first concrete, physically realistic scheme for a quantum computer. Experimental realisations of gates, entanglement and error-corrected operations make this an enduring contribution of atomic physics.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller are clearly decisive on the theory side. Blatt led the experimental realisation (teleportation, multi-ion entanglement, early algorithms). Wineland and Monroe are also central experimentally. Wineland already has the 2012 prize, and Monroe is not in the supplied credits, which could leave the experimental side incomplete.
assessment.maturity: Very mature as physics: more than a quarter century of experiments, with commercial devices. Recognition is arguably overdue, though the quantum-computing narrative is partly still unfolding. The 2022 and 2025 prizes in quantum information science slightly lower the urgency.
uncertainties: Overlap with Wineland's 2012 recognition and with the Monroe/Kielpinski contributions could complicate the allocation.
Zoller also appears under the optical lattice candidate, so the committee must avoid rewarding the same person twice for overlapping ideas.
A separate question is whether quantum computing should wait for a clearer demonstration of practical advantage.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum simulation with ultracold atoms in optical lattices, in particular the observation of the superfluid-to-Mott-insulator transition and then fermionic Hubbard physics and quantum gas microscopes, gave a controllable way to study many-body models. The theoretical bridge (Jaksch et al.) and the experiments together form a coherent, important body of work and a central mission of modern AMO physics.
assessment.attribution: Greiner (with Bloch and Hänsch) did the 2002 Mott insulator experiment; Bloch led the following development of the field; Esslinger led the fermionic Hubbard experiments. Zoller is the theoretical architect, but the 3-person cap means one must choose, and I favour experimentalists here because Zoller fits better under B021. The attribution is hard because Hänsch and Jaksch are not included.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced by many groups, and the techniques are well established. The BEC prize of 2001 provides the backdrop. The research topic is mature, although the claim of useful quantum advantage for simulation is still being tested.
uncertainties: Credit allocation among Bloch, Greiner, Esslinger and Zoller is uncertain.
Whether the committee views this as an extension of the BEC prize and so not distinct enough.
Quantum simulation may still be developing, so the final scientific legacy is not settled.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Matter-wave interferometry with atoms gives inertial sensors, gravimeters, gradiometers and measurements of G and the fine-structure constant, and prospective tests of the equivalence principle and gravitational-wave detection. It is a pillar of precision measurement and shows the coherent control of atomic motion that atomic physics is known for.
assessment.attribution: Bordé made the early theoretical and Ramsey-Bordé interferometer contributions; Pritchard did the first atom interferometer with gratings and pioneered the field; Kasevich realised the light-pulse atom interferometers with high sensitivity. Chu and Cohen-Tannoudji (1997 prize), Chu in particular, are tied to the same techniques, and Ramsey (1989) provides relevant background.
assessment.maturity: Technique is well established and independently confirmed. Applications such as gravimetry and gradiometry are commercial, but the headline fundamental-physics goals (e.g. gravitational waves) are not yet achieved, so the discovery is mature while the highest impact is prospective.
uncertainties: Overlap with Chu's 1997 laser-cooling prize and with Ramsey's 1989 method.
Several others (Chu, Mlynek, Keith, Kasevich-Chu) could fairly be credited; priority is not settled in the text I was given.
Whether a technique, not a single discovery, fits the invention criterion cleanly.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: BB84 and E91 established quantum cryptography, with security grounded in quantum mechanics and Bell-type tests. They are conceptually original and connect directly to the 2022 prize on entangled photons and Bell inequalities. The influence on quantum communication and the foundations of quantum information is large.
assessment.attribution: Bennett and Brassard are the BB84 authors; Ekert proposed entanglement-based E91. Wiesner's earlier conjugate-coding idea is a known priority question. The three supplied names form a plausible and fairly clean configuration.
assessment.maturity: Experimentally verified through many fibre and satellite demonstrations, with commercial systems, though real-world security issues remain at the device level. The theory is mature and recognition is plausible now, but the 2022 prize may reduce the appetite for another award nearby.
uncertainties: Wiesner's priority and the status of his unpublished and delayed paper.
Whether the 2022 prize already covered the central conceptual territory.
Practical security loopholes do not reduce the conceptual contribution but affect how the impact is described.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Single-atom cavity QED in the strong-coupling regime, atom-photon quantum interfaces and the elementary quantum network proposals built on them (state transfer, photon-photon gates, quantum repeater nodes) are a coherent line of work in light-matter interaction, and also of interest to my own interest in quantum memories and repeaters. They have enabled quantum networking concepts.
assessment.attribution: Kimble and Rempe led the pioneering experiments on strong coupling, single-atom control and photon interfaces, and Cirac was the theory partner (quantum state transfer and network proposals). Haroche's 2012 prize overlaps in the cavity QED domain, and Cirac again overlaps with B021.
assessment.maturity: The experiments are mature, but the large-scale quantum network application is still in progress. Recognition would be somewhat early for the network narrative but fine for the basic cavity-QED science.
uncertainties: Overlap with Haroche's prize and with the Cirac-Zoller work in B021.
Whether the 'network' framing is a coherent single discovery or a synthesis of several.
Kimble also appears under the squeezed-light candidate.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The theory of squeezed-state quantum metrology and its experimental implementation, culminating in squeezed-light injection into gravitational-wave interferometers, is a clear case where quantum optics improved a major measurement. Squeezing beyond the standard quantum limit is a core measurement-physics idea.
assessment.attribution: Caves provided the central theory proposal of squeezed vacuum in interferometers; Kimble led the first experimental squeezed-state generation; Schnabel developed the GEO600/LIGO implementation. The 4-person list includes Mavalvala, who is important for LIGO squeezing, so omitting her is a significant attribution choice, and Slusher, Walls and Yuen are not credited.
assessment.maturity: Squeezing is routinely used in LIGO, Virgo and GEO600, so confirmation is strong. LIGO already received the 2017 prize, which tempers novelty but the specific technique is distinct.
uncertainties: Choice among Caves, Kimble, Schnabel and Mavalvala is difficult, and early experimental pioneers (Slusher, Wu, Walls) are absent.
Whether squeezing is seen as an incremental improvement relative to the LIGO prize.
Kimble overlaps with B050.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Trapping, cooling and spectroscopy of antihydrogen and antiprotons, giving tests of CPT and of antimatter gravity, as well as precision comparisons with hydrogen, are demanding laser-spectroscopy and ion-trap experiments with direct links to fundamental symmetry.
assessment.attribution: Hangst leads ALPHA (antihydrogen trapping and 1S-2S spectroscopy), Gabrielse developed antiproton and positron trapping and ATRAP, and Ulmer leads BASE (proton/antiproton magnetic moments). Other collaboration members and the earlier ATHENA team (Amoretti, Fischer) have some claim, and it is not simple to separate collaboration credit from the named individuals.
assessment.maturity: The experimental results are impressive and replicated by several collaborations, but the precision tests have so far shown agreement with CPT, so the physical conclusion is a null result and the field is still advancing.
uncertainties: Large collaborations make credit allocation difficult.
The scientific significance is based on null results at current precision.
Maturity: the most important measurements (gravity, higher-precision spectroscopy) are still ongoing.
